title: Better Schools, Less Crime?
research_question: Does attending a more preferred (higher-quality) middle or high school reduce subsequent involvement in adult criminal activity, and if so, for which youth and through what channels (school quality versus peer composition)? How do gains from access to a preferred school translate into longer-term outcomes such as arrests, incarceration, and educational progression?
data_description: The study links longitudinal administrative records from the Charlotte-Mecklenburg School District (CMS) — covering demographics, addresses, attendance, suspensions, end-of-year test scores in math and reading, and disciplinary incidents from the mid-1990s onward — to adult arrest records from the Mecklenburg County Sheriff's online database, historical arrest records obtained directly from MCS, and incarceration records from the MCS county jail and the North Carolina Department of Corrections. Records are matched by name and date of birth. The unit of observation is an individual student (grades 6–11 in 2001–2002) who applied for the spring 2002 school choice lottery. Outcomes are tracked for seven years after random assignment (through 2009), including arrests by crime type, social cost of crimes, sentence-weighted severity, and days incarcerated. The analytic samples include 1,891 high school and 2,320 middle school lottery applicants.
institutional_context: From 1971 until 2001, CMS operated under a court-ordered busing plan to maintain racial balance. After the order was overturned, in December 2001 the CMS School Board adopted a district-wide open enrollment plan effective for 2002–2003. School boundaries were redrawn into contiguous neighborhood zones with guaranteed access to the home school, and families could submit up to three choices for non-guaranteed schools. About 95% of parents submitted at least one choice and roughly 40% chose a non-guaranteed school. When demand exceeded capacity at a school, slots were allocated by random draws within strictly ordered priority groups (returning students/siblings; low-income applicants to schools with few low-income students; and within-zone applicants), administered centrally with a first-choice maximizer algorithm. Inner-city Charlotte was densely segregated, so many minority and low-income students applied to leave their assigned neighborhood schools.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: RDD — treatment = students attending better schools, control = students attending lower-quality schools; cutoff = school lottery assignment

key_variables.treatment: Assignment to a higher-quality school through the lottery
key_variables.control: Students not assigned to higher-quality schools
key_variables.time_period: 1996 to 1999 for lottery assignment, with long-term follow-up

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Attending a higher-quality school through the lottery significantly reduces subsequent criminal behavior.
